prompt.context: Our client is a large manufacturer of explosive products. Recently, their largest customer, a mining company, has called for a competitive bid for their next 3-year contract. Previously, we have been their preferred provider and have run uncontested.
prompt.question: Our client wants to know how we should price the bid.

clarifying_info.q: What products does our client provide?
clarifying_info.a: Three products: (1) Ammonium nitrate (AN) used to create the explosion, (2) Ignition systems (IS) used to start the explosion, (3) Slot services — contracting services to help clients understand where to place explosives.

clarifying_info.q: Why did the mining company put the contract out to RFP?
clarifying_info.a: We are not sure, but suspect it could be internal cost pressures.

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about the mining firm and their current contract?
clarifying_info.a: The mining firm owns two mines, one in Kentucky and one in Wyoming. Previously, 80% of the revenue from their contract has been derived from AN and 20% from IS. They do not purchase any slot services as they have their own people.

clarifying_info.q: What volumes did they purchase and at what price?
clarifying_info.a: They purchased 40,000 tons of AN at $1,000 per ton and IS at $250 per ton of AN (there is a predetermined ratio of how much IS is needed per ton of AN).
Nothing has changed from a competitive standpoint — the client has the same competitors as always and is generally seen as the market and price leader.

clarifying_info.q: How do our products compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: AN is pretty much a commodity, although we charge about a $10 premium over competitors. From an IS standpoint, we are the clear leader and have a quality product for which customers will pay a premium.

clarifying_info.q: Do all competitors provide both products?
clarifying_info.a: Our largest competitor provides both, although they have bad ignition systems. There are other competitors for IS abroad that are closer in quality to ours. AN can be purchased from many places as it is a commodity.

clarifying_info.q: What are the margins on each product?
clarifying_info.a: AN gets a 20% margin and IS gets an 80% margin.

clarifying_info.q: What are the specifics of the future contract?
clarifying_info.a: It will be for the same components in the same volumes as the current contract.

clarifying_info.q: How much could the mining company save by purchasing products separately?
clarifying_info.a: They could get the next closest IS system for $100 per ton cheaper by purchasing overseas. Additionally, assume they would need 1 person at $100k per year to manage the process.

framework: Analyze external factors: customer needs (past and present), competitive landscape, and industry product mix
Conduct internal analysis of options available to the client, focusing on drivers of profitability
Calculate current contract value and profit by product
Assess the customer's outside options (build vs. buy scenario) to establish a pricing floor
Determine optimal pricing strategy by product, distinguishing commodity (AN) from differentiated (IS) components

questions.prompt: Calculate the current contract revenue and profit breakdown by product.
questions.guidance: AN revenue: 40,000 tons x $1,000 = $40M. IS revenue: 40,000 tons x $250 = $10M. Total revenue = $50M. AN profit: $40M x 20% = $8M. IS profit: $10M x 80% = $8M. Total profit = $16M.

math.setup: Revenue by product, then apply stated margins.
steps: IS revenue = 40,000 tons x $250/ton of AN = $10,000,000
math.answer: Total revenue $50M; total profit $16M ($8M from AN, $8M from IS)

questions.prompt: Estimate how much the mining company could save by sourcing products independently, and assess whether that changes our pricing strategy.
questions.guidance: IS abroad is $100/ton cheaper. Savings on IS = 40,000 x $100 = $4M/year. Internal management cost = $100k/year. Net savings = ~$3.9M/year. However, IS abroad is inferior quality, and the customer likely does not want the complexity of managing it separately. The $100k management cost is negligible versus $16M total profit. Conclusion: no need to advertise the integrated bundle as a premium — focus instead on where to concede price.

math.setup: Customer's alternative: buy IS overseas at $150/ton instead of $250/ton.
steps: IS savings if sourced overseas = 40,000 tons x $100/ton savings = $4,000,000/year
math.answer: Customer could save ~$4M/year by going independent, but faces quality trade-off and management burden

questions.prompt: Recommend a bid price for each product, with reasoning.
questions.guidance: AN is a commodity — little value in discounting it; margins are already low (20%). IS is differentiated, higher margin (80%), and hard for the customer to replace with equivalent quality. The customer's best alternative saves them $4M on IS. Rather than conceding the full $4M, halve the concession to retain value: reduce IS price by $50/ton (from $250 to $200/ton), which reduces IS revenue by $2M/year. This is a strong competitive offer that preserves most of the $8M IS profit. Keep AN at $1,000/ton (commodity benchmark plus modest premium).

math.setup: Reduce IS price by half the customer's potential savings to share value while retaining profit.
math.answer: Bid IS at $200/ton; keep AN at $1,000/ton. Total profit ~$14.4M vs. $16M today — a $1.6M concession to win the contract.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic considerations should the client keep in mind beyond the bid price?

categories.name: Customer retention
ideas: Locking in a 3-year contract secures predictable revenue and protects market share
Losing the contract to a lower-quality competitor could create a precedent for other customers

categories.name: Competitive signaling
ideas: As market and price leader, aggressive discounting could trigger price wars across the customer base
Selective discounting (IS only) is less visible to the market than cutting AN, which is commodity-priced

categories.name: Value communication
ideas: Emphasize quality advantage of IS versus overseas alternatives
Quantify risk and management burden of split sourcing to justify integrated premium

categories.name: Relationship dynamics
ideas: Investigate root cause of RFP — if cost pressure is temporary, a modest one-time concession may suffice
Consider non-price levers: contract flexibility, service levels, or added slot services

categories.name: Cost management
ideas: Explore whether cost reductions in AN production could preserve margin even at a lower price
Assess whether volume commitments from the 3-year contract justify supply chain investments

recommendation: Bid IS at $200/ton (a $50/ton reduction from current $250/ton) and maintain AN at $1,000/ton
This shares roughly half the customer's potential savings from self-sourcing, making the integrated offer compelling while preserving ~$14.4M in annual profit versus $16M today
risks: Customer may still push for further concessions once they see our willingness to reduce price
Overseas IS competitors may improve quality over the 3-year contract period, eroding our differentiation
Internal cost pressures at the mining firm may be more severe than assumed, requiring larger concessions to win
next_steps: Verify the customer's true motivations for the RFP through relationship channels before submitting the bid
Model scenarios: win at $200/ton vs. lose the contract entirely — weigh foregone $14.4M profit against cost of losing the account
Consider bundling slot services at no charge as a value-add to differentiate the bid without further price cuts
